content.title: Deleting Off-Topic and Repetitive Information
content.overview: Effective writing requires focus and economy. On the ACT, you must identify and remove sentences or phrases that distract from the main idea (off-topic) or restate information already provided (repetitive).
learning_objectives: Identify sentences that shift focus away from the paragraph's main idea.
Recognize and eliminate redundant phrasing that repeats earlier information.
Evaluate whether a sentence provides essential support or merely distracting detail.
Ensure paragraph flow and transitions remain intact after deleting irrelevant content.

sections.title: The Trim-to-Topic Strategy
sections.content: The ACT tests your ability to maintain a tight focus. To decide if a sentence should be deleted, ask: 'Does this unit add new, specific support or clarify the topic sentence?' If the answer is no, the information is likely irrelevant. Off-topic content often introduces a different subject or a minor anecdotal detail that doesn't serve the paragraph's primary purpose. Even if a detail is interesting or 'colorful,' it should be removed if it distracts from the central argument or description.

sections.title: Identifying Redundancy
sections.content: Redundancy occurs when a sentence or phrase restates an idea that has already been established without adding new evidence or clarity. When you encounter repetition, you should delete the weaker or redundant phrasing and keep the clearer, more concise statement. A common ACT trap is providing a sentence that is technically true but adds nothing new to the reader's understanding.

sections.title: The Final Check: Flow and Transition
sections.content: Before finalizing a deletion, perform a 'Final Check.' Read the paragraph (mentally) without the suspect sentence. Ensure that the transition between the preceding and following sentences is still logical and smooth. The goal is to tighten the focus while preserving all essential facts and necessary transitions.

worked_examples.question:
Many communities rely on local parks for recreation and social events. They offer trails, playgrounds, and open fields for exercise. [The park also has a food truck that serves tacos and local crafts are sold nearby, which some people enjoy.] Park programs schedule classes and volunteer cleanups throughout the year. 

Should the bracketed sentence be kept or deleted?
worked_examples.solution: 1. Identify the main idea: The paragraph focuses on how parks provide general recreation and organized programs. 2. Evaluate the bracketed sentence: It describes a specific food truck and craft sales. While these are 'park-related,' they are anecdotal details that do not support the broader point of recreation and programming. 3. Check for distraction: The sentence shifts focus to specific vendors. 4. Conclusion: Delete the sentence because it is a distracting detail unrelated to the paragraph’s main point.

worked_examples.question: The architect designed the skyscraper to be environmentally sustainable. She included solar panels on the roof and a rainwater collection system. [The building was created in a way that would not harm the environment and would last a long time.] These features reduced the building's carbon footprint significantly.
worked_examples.solution: 1. Identify the main idea: The paragraph describes specific sustainable features of a building. 2. Evaluate the bracketed sentence: It states the building was 'created in a way that would not harm the environment.' 3. Check for redundancy: The first sentence already established that the building is 'environmentally sustainable.' The bracketed sentence repeats this concept without adding new details. 4. Conclusion: Delete the sentence because it is redundant.

common_mistakes: Keeping 'interesting' details: Students often keep sentences because they contain fun facts, even if those facts don't support the paragraph's specific goal.
Mistaking length for strength: Thinking a longer paragraph is more persuasive, leading to the retention of redundant sentences.
Ignoring transitions: Deleting a sentence that actually serves as a necessary bridge between two different ideas.
exam_tips: If a sentence feels like a 'side note' or a 'by the way' comment, it is likely off-topic.
Watch for synonyms; if a sentence uses different words to say exactly what the previous sentence said, it is redundant.
Always ask: 'If I take this out, does the reader lose any essential information?' If the answer is no, delete it.
content.recap: To master topic development, use the Trim-to-Topic strategy: remove any sentence that fails to advance the main idea or repeats information already stated. Always ensure the remaining text flows logically and retains its essential meaning.

knowledge_claims.content: To determine if a sentence should be deleted, ask if it adds new, specific support or clarifies the topic sentence.
Off-topic content is information that introduces a different subject or anecdotal detail that does not advance the paragraph's main idea.
Redundancy is the restatement of an idea using different words without adding new evidence or clarity.
When two sentences repeat the same information, the weaker or redundant phrasing should be deleted in favor of the clearer statement.
A final check for deletion involves reading the paragraph to ensure transitions remain logical and essential facts are preserved.
It is a mistake to keep a sentence simply because it adds 'community color' or interesting details if those details distract from the main focus.
A sentence that shifts from general functions to a specific, unrelated anecdote is a signal for potential deletion.
Removing irrelevant or redundant text is intended to tighten the focus and improve the clarity of the paragraph's support for its main idea.
If a sentence provides a 'side note' that does not strengthen the topic sentence's point, it should be marked for deletion.
Essential transitions must be distinguished from irrelevant details; transitions bridge ideas, while irrelevant details distract from them.
Information that is technically true but adds nothing new to the reader's understanding of the topic should be removed.
Redundancy can be recognized by identifying synonyms that restate the previous sentence's core message.

items.stem:
ENGLISH PASSAGE 1: The Clock Above Alder Street
[1] After three months of fundraising [[a neighborhood restoration crew began]] to repair the brass clock above Alder Street Market. Before beginning, the group listed what it already knew, what would need to be measured, and which decisions could still be reversed without damaging the project. [2] A series of early sketches [[were]] pinned beside photographs of a market hall built in 1911, giving the work a visible history. Visitors could follow the sequence from initial assumption to later revision, and several left written questions that the group discussed at the next session. [3] Using a laser scan and a box of hand-labeled gears, [[the first set of observations was recorded by the team]] before any permanent change was made. [4] The procedure initially seemed straightforward. [[However]] wear marks showed that an earlier repairer had reversed two nearly identical wheels. Rather than treat that detail as a nuisance, the group compared it with the earlier records and checked whether the same pattern appeared under a second set of conditions. [5] When the team discussed the evidence with visitors, [[they]] asked questions that revealed which parts of the explanation remained unclear. [6] The group could have ignored the complication [[it instead treated the problem as useful evidence]]. That decision slowed the schedule by several days, but it also produced a clearer record of why one approach had been rejected and another adopted. [7] That choice was [[completely essential and absolutely necessary]] because replacement parts would have erased those clues. [8] The records were especially [[nice]]: they showed why the crew cleaned and reused the original wheels. The team also saved measurements from the unsuccessful version, since those values might help another group recognize the same limitation sooner. [9] The writer is considering adding this sentence here: “Every tool was returned to a labeled drawer at the end of each session.” [10] Ultimately, the clock kept accurate time through a week of rain. [[The most effective conclusion should emphasize that the repair preserved evidence of how local mechanics once solved problems.]]

Should the writer add the proposed sentence in [9]?
A) No, because the detail about tool storage distracts from the explanation of how evidence changed the project.
B) Yes, because any concrete detail makes an informational passage stronger.
C) Yes, because the sentence proves that the project used expensive equipment.
D) No, because ACT passages should never mention routine procedures.

options.A: No, because the detail about tool storage distracts from the explanation of how evidence changed the project.
options.B: Yes, because any concrete detail makes an informational passage stronger.
options.C: Yes, because the sentence proves that the project used expensive equipment.
options.D: No, because ACT passages should never mention routine procedures.

items.explanation: The paragraph focuses on interpreting evidence and revising the project; tool storage does not develop that focus.

ENGLISH PASSAGE 2: Counting After Dark
[1] After several cloudy evenings [[a coastal ecology class began]] to count juvenile crabs in tide pools after sunset. Before beginning, the group listed what it already knew, what would need to be measured, and which decisions could still be reversed without damaging the project. [2] A series of early sketches [[were]] pinned beside photographs of a protected inlet beside the school, giving the work a visible history. Visitors could follow the sequence from initial assumption to later revision, and several left written questions that the group discussed at the next session. [3] Using red lamps, quadrats, and waterproof tally sheets, [[the first set of observations was recorded by the team]] before any permanent change was made. [4] The procedure initially seemed straightforward. [[However]] the smallest crabs appeared most often under flat stones near eelgrass. Rather than treat that detail as a nuisance, the group compared it with the earlier records and checked whether the same pattern appeared under a second set of conditions. [5] When the team discussed the evidence with visitors, [[they]] asked questions that revealed which parts of the explanation remained unclear. [6] The group could have ignored the complication [[it instead treated the problem as useful evidence]]. That decision slowed the schedule by several days, but it also produced a clearer record of why one approach had been rejected and another adopted. [7] That choice was [[completely essential and absolutely necessary]] because bright white light changed the animals’ movement. [8] The records were especially [[nice]]: they showed why the class switched to dim red lamps and repeated the first survey. The team also saved measurements from the unsuccessful version, since those values might help another group recognize the same limitation sooner. [9] The writer is considering adding this sentence here: “Every tool was returned to a labeled drawer at the end of each session.” [10] Ultimately, the second set of counts was more consistent. [[The most effective conclusion should emphasize that the revised method gave park staff a dependable baseline for future surveys.]]

A) Yes, because any concrete detail makes an informational passage stronger.
B) Yes, because the sentence proves that the project used expensive equipment.
C) No, because the detail about tool storage distracts from the explanation of how evidence changed the project.
D) No, because ACT passages should never mention routine procedures.

videoLesson.title: Trim Off-Topic, Repetitive, or Irrelevant Details
videoLesson.description: You will recognize sentences that add no new support or repeat earlier wording. Delete units that neither clarify the topic sentence nor provide essential transitions or necessary detail.
